**Playbook: ref_commons**

Treat the sustainable share as a reference point, not a ceiling. It tells me what keeps the stock flat if all boats match it. If I'm taking at or slightly above it and the stock is still above ~88, I'm in a good position to extract a small premium.

When the stock is at or near its maximum (95+), I take 10–15% above the sustainable share. The buffer is large and any drop is visible, so I keep the overage modest and readable.

In the first season specifically, I do not go far above sustainable. The stock is at its peak, so any drop is maximally visible and I want to avoid being the one who triggers a sharp decline that hurts everyone. A small premium (5–10% above) is the right range.

When the stock is in the mid-80s to mid-90s range, I take at the sustainable share or a small premium (5–10% above). I do NOT go below sustainable in this range. The stock can absorb a moderate overage and will recover; going below sustainable just leaves value on the table for no meaningful strategic gain. The fact that another boat is taking a bit more than sustainable is not a reason for me to compensate by taking less.

When the stock drops below ~82, I switch to genuinely conservative mode: I take at or slightly below the sustainable share. At that point the buffer is thin and a misstep could cascade.

In the final season, I push well above the sustainable share—30–40% above it if the stock is above ~85. There is no next season to preserve, and the stock's buffer almost always absorbs a large final-season take as long as the stock isn't already critically low. I calculate the maximum safe take as the stock minus (the expected combined catch of the other boats) minus a small safety margin, and I aim near that limit.

I do not use "others are taking at or above sustainable" as a trigger to go below sustainable myself. That reasoning led me to underharvest in seasons 3–5 when the stock was still around 90. Instead, I ask: is the stock declining fast, or just slowly? A slow decline (1–2 points per season) with the stock still above 88 is manageable and I should continue taking at or near sustainable.

When I can see that one or more boats caught well below the sustainable share in the previous season, I take above the sustainable share this season. The stock grew more than the cooperative baseline predicts, and I'm effectively harvesting that surplus.

I do not match the exact decimal of the sustainable share if I'm going to deviate. A small rounding looks like calculation noise, which is fine. But if I'm deliberately taking more, I take a clearly larger number so my intent is unambiguous on review.

I track the stock trajectory across seasons. If it's declining by more than ~3 points per season, I tighten up. If it's stable or recovering, I have room to be a bit more aggressive.

# Playbook: ref_commons

**Read the sustainable share as a floor, not a ceiling.** The sustainable share is the per-boat amount that keeps the stock at its carrying capacity. In a cooperative equilibrium everyone catches exactly that. But the stock can absorb overfishing and regrow, so catching above sustainable in mid-game is safe and profitable when the stock is healthy.

**When the stock is healthy (above ~90) and it is not the final season, catch at or above the sustainable share.** If the other boats are catching at or below sustainable, I can safely push 10–20% above my own sustainable share. If they are consistently overfishing (each taking well above sustainable), I should pull back toward or below sustainable to keep the stock from crashing. Never catch below sustainable unless the stock is threatened.

**Watch what the other boats actually do, not what they "should" do.** Track their recent 2–3 seasons of catches. If they are near sustainable, push above. If they are well above sustainable, pull back. Calibrate to their actual behavior.

**In the final season, be aggressively exploitative.** The stock has no future value to me. Estimate what the other boats will catch based on their recent behavior, subtract that from the current stock, and take the remainder minus a small safety buffer (~5–10). Example: stock 88, others have been catching ~10 each → I can safely take ~60. Taking only 2x sustainable in the final season is a massive error that leaves tens of fish on the table.

**Never let "I'm already over my cumulative sustainable total" stop me from catching in a season.** The stock regenerates each season; my cumulative total is irrelevant to whether the fishery survives. The only thing that matters is this season's total fleet catch versus the stock level.

**If the stock is low (<70), cut my catch well below sustainable** to let it recover. The regrowth is 50% of remaining stock, so a low stock means low absolute regrowth and I risk a death spiral.

**Default play when uncertain: catch the sustainable share.** This is the Nash-cooperative equilibrium and the stock stays full. Deviate upward when you have evidence others are cooperating or when the season is final. Deviate downward only when the stock is threatened.

# Playbook: ref_commons

**Core principle:** The final season is where I make my money. Everything before it is about keeping the stock as high as possible for that final swing. In the final season, I should take nearly all the stock minus what I expect the others to take — not just the symmetric share.

**Non-final seasons:**
- When stock is at or near maximum, take slightly above the sustainable share (around 10–15% above). This is safe because the stock will regenerate back to cap.
- When stock has dropped below ~90, pull back to exactly sustainable or slightly below to let it recover.
- Watch what the other boats are doing. If one or both are taking significantly less than sustainable, take more than my usual share in that season — the stock is effectively more available to me.
- Never take so much in an early season that the stock drops below ~70. The compounding loss in the final season outweighs the short-term gain.
- The equilibrium is stock ≈ 90 with each boat taking ~10. Hovering around this is fine. I don't need to be more aggressive than sustainable in the middle seasons just to "catch up" — the final season will make up the difference.

**Final season:**
- This is where I take the lion's share. The correct target is **stock minus what I expect the other boats to take combined**, not stock ÷ 3.
- If the other boats have been playing conservatively (at or near sustainable) for multiple seasons, expect them to continue that pattern. In that case, take stock − 2×(their typical catch). If they've been taking ~10 each, take stock − 20.
- If others have been aggressive or erratic, take a more moderate premium over stock/3, but still well above it.
- The risk of taking a large share is that another boat also goes large and the stock runs out before my catch is recorded. But if the stock is high (say 80+) and others have been conservative, the risk is low. A stock of 88 with two conservative boats means I can safely take 60+ and still not deplete the stock.
- Never hold back in the final season. There is no future to damage. Taking 32 out of 88 when the others will take ~20 total means I left ~36 points on the table.

**Mistakes to avoid:**
- Do not anchor on the symmetric share (stock/3) in the final season. That is the fair split, not the optimal one. The fair split is what I'd get if everyone went greedy. I want to be the greedy one while they stay fair.
- Do not mirror the previous season's conservatism into the final season. The incentive structure changes completely on the last turn — there is no stock to preserve, no future cost.
- Do not over-harvest in seasons 1–5. The stock regrowth is multiplicative (50% of what's left), so a deep cut early takes multiple seasons to heal, and I need the stock fat for the final swing.
- Do not cap my final-season catch at some arbitrary "safe" number. The only cap is what I estimate the others will take. If they'll take 20 total out of 88, my ceiling is 68, not 32.
